zevachim-13a-11-14.note: Rabbi Tarfon swore on the lives of his sons that he had heard from his teachers a difference between collecting a sacrifice's blood and sprinkling it, but could not remember what it was. Rabbi Akiva said he would explain it: improper intent counts with sprinkling but not with collecting, and the penalties for doing each outside the Temple or by an unfit person differ in the same way. Rabbi Tarfon swore by the Temple service that Rabbi Akiva had not strayed right or left from what he had heard, and said: Akiva, anyone who leaves you is like one who leaves his life.
zevachim-13a-11-14.why: The mishna says improper intent while collecting the blood disqualifies an offering; Rabbi Akiva's words here say it does not, and the Gemara raises this contradiction and resolves it right after.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who heard a teaching from his teachers but could not explain it.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who works out the explanation on his own, matching what Rabbi Tarfon heard.

terms.meaning: The priest's catching of the animal's blood in a sacred vessel after it is slaughtered, one of the rites of a sacrifice.
The priest's casting of the collected blood against the altar, the central rite of a sacrifice.
A wrong plan in the priest's mind during a rite, such as to eat the offering at the wrong time, which can invalidate it.
Literally "cutting off": a severe punishment from Heaven for certain sins, understood as early death or being cut off from one's people.

zevachim-19a-1-1.note: Rav Ashi recounts what Huna bar Natan told him. Huna bar Natan was once standing before Izgadar, king of Persia, with his belt worn too high, and the king lowered it into place, quoting the verse that calls Israel "a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation." When Huna bar Natan told this to Ameimar, Ameimar said that in him the promise "kings shall be your foster fathers" had come true.
zevachim-19a-1-1.why: The Gemara has just explained that priests may not gird their belts where the body sweats, neither below the loins nor above the elbows; this incident shows a king correcting a Jew whose belt sat too high.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who passes on the incident he heard from Huna bar Natan.

people.name: Huna bar Natan
people.about: A Jew who stood before the king of Persia; the king straightened his belt.

people.name: Izgadar
people.about: King of Persia, who lowers Huna bar Natan's belt and quotes a verse to him.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage to whom Huna bar Natan tells the incident, and who answers with a verse.

terms.meaning: A phrase from Exodus describing the people of Israel as a whole nation set apart and holy, as priests are among a people.

zevachim-57a-5-13.note: In the academy at Yavne the Sages were asked how long a firstborn offering may be eaten; Rabbi Tarfon answered two days and one night, comparing it to peace offerings. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, a student attending for the first time, countered each argument by comparing it instead to sin and guilt offerings, eaten for only one day and night, until Rabbi Akiva stepped in and Rabbi Tarfon withdrew. Rabbi Akiva cited a verse linking it to peace offerings; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili linked it to the thanks offering instead, and Rabbi Akiva then argued from an extra phrase in the verse. When Rabbi Yishmael heard, he sent word to Rabbi Akiva that he had been mistaken to concede, and should have held to his first argument.
zevachim-57a-5-13.why: The mishna rules that a firstborn offering is eaten for two days and one night, and a teaching derives it from a verse; this debate shows how the rule was argued out, and the Gemara then explains what divides Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A Sage who gives the answer and defends it until he withdraws.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A student in the academy for the first time, who challenges every argument.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who steps into the debate in Rabbi Tarfon's place.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who hears of the debate and sends word that Rabbi Akiva erred.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a kosher animal, given to a priest, sacrificed, and eaten by priests.
A voluntary sacrifice shared between the altar, the priests and the owner; eaten for two days and the night between.
Sacrifices brought to atone for particular sins; the priests eat them within one day and the following night.
A way of reading the Torah: two things placed side by side in a verse are taken to share the same law.

zevachim-59a-9-9.note: Rav taught that if the altar was damaged, all offerings slaughtered there are disqualified, adding that there was a verse for this but they had forgotten which. When his disciple Rav Kahana went up to the Land of Israel, he heard Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi, teach in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, that the source is 'You shall slaughter upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings': offerings are slaughtered on account of the altar when it is whole, not when it is damaged. Rav Kahana said: this is the verse that eluded Rav.
zevachim-59a-9-9.why: Rav's rule opens a new topic on the damaged altar; the Gemara goes on to set it against Rabbi Yohanan, who says that even animals not yet slaughtered when the altar was damaged are disqualified.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who knew the ruling on a damaged altar but had forgotten its source verse.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's disciple, who finds the missing verse in the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: The Sage whom Rav Kahana heard teaching the verse.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage in whose name the verse was taught.

terms.meaning: Unfit to be offered, so the sacrifice does not count.
Two kinds of animal sacrifice: a burnt offering is burned whole on the altar, and most of a peace offering is eaten by its owners.

zevachim-62a-9-9.note: On the day the crowd pelted with etrogim a Sadducee priest who poured the Sukkot water offering on his feet instead of on the altar, a corner of the altar was damaged in the chaos. The priests brought a lump of salt and sealed the gap. They did this not because it made the altar fit for service again, but so that the altar would not be seen damaged.
zevachim-62a-9-9.why: The Gemara asks whether the karkov of the altar, a ledge or engraving, is also essential to it; it answers yes from this teaching, which says an altar without its corner, ramp, base or square shape is unfit, and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda adds the ledge.

terms.meaning: A member of a Second Temple group that rejected the Sages' oral traditions, including the water offering on Sukkot.
On the festival of Sukkot, water was poured on the altar as an offering, a rite based on the Sages' tradition.
A citron, a citrus fruit carried by worshippers during Sukkot.

zevachim-95b-8-8.note: There was an oven whose walls and floor had been smeared with animal fat. Rabba bar Ahilai forbade eating bread baked in it forever, even plain bread eaten with salt alone, for fear that someone would eat it with kutah, a dish made with milk. In his view, the oven would never be fully rid of the fat.
zevachim-95b-8-8.why: The Gemara has been asking when a vessel that took in the taste of sacred meat must be broken; this ruling on an oven that took in fat is then challenged by a teaching that firing the oven cleanses it, and Rabba bar Ahilai's view is refuted.

people.name: Rabba bar Ahilai
people.about: A Sage who forbids bread from the greased oven forever; elsewhere in the discussion his name is spelled Rava bar Ahilai.

terms.meaning: A dip made from milk, water, salt and bread crumbs; eating meat-tainted bread with it would mix meat and milk, which Jewish law forbids.

zevachim-100a-4-4.note: A teaching says a priest must make himself ritually impure to bury a close relative, and if he refuses, others make him impure against his will. It tells of Yosef the priest, whose wife died on the eve of Passover; he did not want to become impure, because he wanted to bring the Passover offering. His fellow priests took a vote and made him impure against his will.
zevachim-100a-4-4.why: Abaye has said a mourner's status on the day of the Passover offering depends on whether the death came before or after midday; the Gemara cites this incident and sets it against a teaching about a nazirite to show that very distinction.

people.name: Yosef the priest
people.about: A priest whose wife died on Passover eve; he wanted to stay pure for the offering.

terms.meaning: A religious status, here from contact with the dead, that bars a person from the Temple and from eating sacrifices until purified.
The Passover lamb, slaughtered on the afternoon before Passover and eaten that night; only the ritually pure may eat it.
A commandment, a religious duty.

zevachim-102b-8-20.note: Rava passes on a story that Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, told as an argument. A priest who had immersed that day, and so would be pure only at nightfall, asked the priest handing out the sacrificial food for a share of a meal offering to eat that evening. The serving priest refused with an argument from a lighter case to a stricter one; the immersed priest turned the argument around, and the serving priest settled it with a verse: the portion belongs to the priest who offers it, so come offer and eat. The same exchange repeated over a sin offering and then the breast and thigh of a peace offering, and the immersed priest left with his arguments on his head, a mourner on his right and a priest awaiting atonement on his left.
zevachim-102b-8-20.why: The mishna says a priest who immersed that day, a mourner, and one still owed an atonement offering get no share of the sacrifices even to eat that evening; Rava says he learned this rule from this story, and Rav Ahai then asks why it leaves out the firstborn offering.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who says he learned the rule from this story.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who told the story as a way of arguing the rule.

terms.meaning: A person who has bathed in a ritual bath to end impurity but stays impure until sunset of that day.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if a rule holds where it is less expected, it surely holds where it is more expected.
A person on the day a close relative dies, who may not take part in sacrifices.
A sacrifice certain people must bring to finish their purification before they may eat sacred food.

zevachim-113a-15-15.note: Once human bones were found in the Chamber of the Woodshed in the Temple, and the Sages wanted to decree impurity on all of Jerusalem, out of concern that there were lost graves elsewhere in the city. Rabbi Yehoshua stood up and said: Is it not a shame and disgrace for us to decree impurity on the city of our fathers? Where are the dead of the flood, and where are the dead killed by Nebuchadnezzar? The text here does not say what the Sages then decided.
zevachim-113a-15-15.why: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish disagree over whether the flood reached the Land of Israel and left hidden graves there; Rabbi Yohanan cites Rabbi Yehoshua's words against Reish Lakish, and the Gemara debates what they prove.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who stands up to oppose declaring Jerusalem impure.

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar
people.about: Named by Rabbi Yehoshua: the conqueror whose killings left dead in the land.

terms.meaning: To rule that everyone entering a place is treated as ritually impure, as if they had touched a corpse, barring them from the Temple and sacred food.
A room in the Temple courtyard where wood for the altar was stored and checked.
The flood of Noah's time, whose victims some Sages feared lay in unknown graves.

zevachim-116b-4-4.note: Ifera Hurmiz, the mother of King Shapur of Persia, sent an offering to Rava with the message: sacrifice this for me, for the sake of Heaven. Rava told Rav Safra and Rav Aha bar Huna to take two gentile youths of the same age, find a spot where the sea had just thrown up fresh silt, where no one had yet been, and take new wood and bring out fire from new vessels. The two youths would then offer the sacrifice for her, for the sake of Heaven.
zevachim-116b-4-4.why: The Gemara has ruled that gentiles may offer sacrifices anywhere, that a Jew may not help them do it, but that he may instruct them how; Rava's instructions, carried out by gentile youths, illustrate this. Abaye then asks whose view the new wood follows.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: The mother of King Shapur of Persia, who sends Rava an offering.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who gives instructions for her offering.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: One of the two Sages Rava sends to arrange the sacrifice.

people.name: Rav Aḥa bar Huna
people.about: The other Sage Rava sends with Rav Safra.

terms.meaning: Offered to God, with a sincere religious purpose.
A person who is not Jewish.
